newsitem.title: GERMANY: German steel giants prefer co-operation to bid battle.
newsitem.headline: German steel giants prefer co-operation to bid battle.

text.p: Germany's two largest steel makers shied away from a bloody bid battle on Monday and sought to find a basis for co-operation instead.

After almost a week of intense pressure from politicians and demonstrations by thousands of workers outraged at what they called its "Wild West" tactics, steel group Krupp AG withdrew plans to take over Thyssen AG.
The firms said they were exploring a co-operation deal which would go beyond a merger of their steel activities and agreed this would enable Germany to survive as a steel production centre.
"The German public sees things very strongly from a social point of view and this led to heavy political pressure," said Mathias Haffner, an economist at BZW in Frankfurt.
Krupp, the full name of which is Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, said its takeover bid was now void and would not be renewed in future.
Such bids are rare here and bankers had welcomed it as an opportunity for Germany's financial centre to prove it could follow the Anglo-Saxon example of a public takeover.

But the bid raised fears of major job losses in the Ruhr region, Germany's industrial heartland, and banks appear to have misjudged public opinion at a time when the country is battling against its worst unemployment in postwar history.

Thyssen's works council chairman said a demonstration by 30,000 workers planned for Tuesday in Frankfurt would go ahead despite Krupp's bid withdrawal, in part to set a signal against the "Americanisation" of German society.

Meanwhile Chancellor Helmut Kohl in a newspaper interview published on Sunday exhorted the companies to shun "pure market economics" and adhere the German spirit of the social market economy to find a solution that was in the workers' interest.

In a further sign of consensus building, the countries' two largest building groups, Holzmann AG and Hochtief AG , looked set on Monday to end a two-and-a-half year battle with a deal paving the way for cooperation abroad.
Analysts say public fear of unemployment, which now stands at 4.7 million, and anger at the government for failing to stem the rise is impairing Bonn's ability to push through structural reforms.
Two weeks ago miners marched on Bonn's government quarter, angry about losing jobs as government subsidies are cut.
And thousands of construction workers stormed the site of the future parliament building in Berlin to protest against a slump that may make almost 100,000 of them unemployed this year.
The miners won extra cash, and the builders a pledge of a 25-billion-mark ($14.8 billion) credit package to boost construction.

Tuesday's demonstration by Thyssen workers looks set to paralyse traffic in Frankfurt's city centre as workers will march to the banking district and stage a rally near Deutsche Bank AG's twin-towered headquarters.
Deutsche, Dresdner Bank AG and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs advised Krupp in its bid for Thyssen.
They have been accused by politicians and union leaders of joining a corporate raid that goes against the grain of Germany's consensus culture and which could cause heavy job losses.
But Deutsche on Monday hit back against criticism that it had engaged in "Wild West" tactics.
"Talk by some politicians and trade unionists of conspiracy theories, Wild West manners, and claims to power by banks, lacks any foundation," it said in a statement. ($ = 1.691 German Marks) REUTER
